rv.q: Platt is superb, bringing his vocal range and agility to Sonnenblick's nostalgic songs.
Platt is Trevor Copeland, a crooning bar-singer reliving the years he spent with songwriter Arthur Brightman, played with plate-spinning brilliance by Gregor Milne.
He's simultaneously charismatic and achingly vulnerable, sending a gorgeous shiver through every song or landing a wisecrack with a practised twinkle.
Platt's sheer star power makes it a night to remember.
A thread of martyred schmaltz runs through Mark Sonnenblick's polished, cabaret-style musical about a gay lounge duo in 1960s Manhattan.

Sonnenblick’s songs – impressively drawing on the traditions of the Great American Songbook – have a maturity that’s a world away from his fizzy earworms for Netflix’s KPop Demon Hunters and prove his range as a composer.

Thematically, Midnight at the Never Get ultimately sides with radicalism, showing how hiding your true self can poison a life. But structurally, it's frustratingly old school – imprisoned by a wistful nostalgia that won't allow Platt's real talents to break free.
It's a lost world evoked in immaculate detail in David Cromer's production: a bold, unconventional drama that doesn't, in the end, pay quite as much attention to the inner lives of the two lovers.
As Trevor, Platt delivers a performance that rattles your bones and stirs your soul.
Platt's vibrato-tinged voice is perfectly suited to the material and it's a joy to witness his talents from such close quarters.
This is a rare opportunity to see a singular talent at the top of his game giving full virtuoso flex to material that feels ripe with embryonic potential.

The burgeoning formation of the American gay identity spills into the relationship between the two men. Arthur's assimilationist approach to his sexuality – "who I am is more than who I f*ck, I make art" – clashes with Trevor's increasing sympathy with gay liberation and other civil rights movements.
This production is as special as theatre gets, furthered by Ben Platt's phenomenal performance.
I truly, wholeheartedly believe that I have seen something that can and should fundamentally shape the next stage of West End theatre.
By the last ten minutes you really, really mind.

cn.t: Critics praise this intimate 1960s cabaret musical for Ben Platt's spellbinding performance and metatheatrical storytelling about queer love and memory, though some find it overly sentimental. The Menier's atmospheric staging earns widespread acclaim.
